questions.question: What are strong parameters in Rails?
questions.title: Strong Parameters
questions.direct_answer: Strong params (Rails 4+) prevent mass-assignment vulnerabilities by requiring you to explicitly permit which fields can be set from user input. `params.require(:user).permit(:name, :email)` allows only name and email through — any other key (like :admin) is filtered out. Without it, `User.create(params[:user])` would let a user set any column, including admin (mass-assignment attack). `require` raises if the key is missing; `permit` returns an ActionController::Parameters that's been 'permitted' (marked safe for mass-assignment). You put it in the controller: `def user_params; params.require(:user).permit(:name, :email, :age); end` then `User.create(user_params)`. Nested: `permit(:name, address: [:city, :zip])`. It enforces a whitelist at the boundary — only the fields you list can reach your models.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you know strong params require+permit to whitelist which fields mass-assignment allows, preventing setting :admin.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Passing raw params to create/update (mass-assignment vulnerability — use permit).
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Strong params: params.require(:user).permit(:name, :email). Whitelist mass-assignment fields; blocks :admin etc. require raises if missing.

sections.title: Whitelist at the Boundary
sections.content: Strong params (Rails 4 plus) prevent mass-assignment vulnerabilities by requiring you to explicitly permit which fields can be set from user input. params require user permit name email allows only name and email through — any other key (like admin) is filtered out. Without it, User create params user would let a user set any column, including admin (mass-assignment attack). require raises if the key is missing; permit returns an ActionController Parameters that's been permitted (marked safe for mass-assignment). You put it in the controller: def user params; params require user permit name email age; end then User create user params. Nested: permit name address city zip. It enforces a whitelist at the boundary — only the fields you list can reach your models.

sections.title: Strong Params
sections.content:
params.require(:user).permit(:name, :email). Whitelist; blocks :admin. require raises if missing.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  R[params.require :user] --> M[raises if :user missing]
  P[.permit name email] --> W[whitelist]
  W --> F[filters out :admin]
  O[other keys] --> D[dropped]
```

sections.title: Strong params
sections.content:
```ruby
class UsersController < ApplicationController
  def create
    # BAD: User.create(params[:user])  -- mass-assignment vulnerability
    #   a user could send user[admin]=1 and become admin!
    @user = User.create(user_params)   # GOOD: only permitted fields
    redirect_to @user
  end

  # The whitelist (the boundary):
  def user_params
    # require(:user) raises if :user is missing
    # permit(...) returns only those keys; others are DROPPED
    params.require(:user).permit(:name, :email, :age)
  end
end

# What gets through:
#   { user: { name:, email:, age:, admin: 1 } }
#   -> user_params returns { name:, email:, age: }  (admin DROPPED)

# require raises if the top key is missing:
#   params.require(:user)  ->  ActionController::ParameterMissing if no :user

# Nested attributes:
params.require(:user).permit(:name, address: [:city, :zip])
#   -> { name:, address: { city:, zip: } }

# Permit all of a sub-hash (careful!):
params.require(:user).permit(:name, tags: [])

# permit returns a 'permitted' ActionController::Parameters (safe for mass-assignment).
# params (unpermitted) raises ActiveModel::ForbiddenAttributesError if passed to create.

# It enforces a WHITELIST at the boundary — only listed fields reach models.
```

sections.title: Common Mistakes
items: Passing raw params to create/update (mass-assignment — set any column, e.g. :admin).
Forgetting require (no error on missing key — silent bug).
Permitting everything (permit! or broad lists) — defeats the purpose.

sections.title: Key Takeaways
items: Strong params require you to explicitly permit which fields mass-assignment allows.
params.require(:user).permit(:name, :email) — only name and email pass; :admin is dropped.
require raises ActionController::ParameterMissing if the key is missing.
permit returns a 'permitted' Parameters object (safe for mass-assignment).
Without it, User.create(params[:user]) lets a user set any column (mass-assignment attack).

sections.title: Spoken Answer
sections.content: Strong params (Rails 4 plus) prevent mass-assignment vulnerabilities by requiring you to explicitly permit which fields can be set from user input. params require user permit name email allows only name and email through — any other key (like admin) is filtered out. Without it, User create params user would let a user set any column, including admin (mass-assignment attack). require raises if the key is missing; permit returns an ActionController Parameters that's been permitted (marked safe for mass-assignment). You put it in the controller: def user params; params require user permit name email age; end then User create user params. Nested: permit name address city zip. It enforces a whitelist at the boundary — only the fields you list can reach your models. A common mistake is passing raw params to create or update, a mass-assignment vulnerability, and forgetting require, which raises if the key is missing.
